lesson.title: Three Pairs, One Powerful Bond: Triple Bonds Explained
lesson.summary: A triple bond is a covalent bond formed by sharing three pairs of electrons between two atoms, making it shorter and stronger than a single or double bond, as in nitrogen gas and acetylene.
lesson.body:
In a Lewis structure, a triple bond appears as three lines connecting two atoms, representing six shared electrons rather than the two electrons of a single bond or the four electrons of a double bond. Like all covalent bonds, a triple bond exists because sharing electrons lets both atoms complete their octets while the buildup of negative charge between the two positively charged nuclei holds the atoms together. The more electron pairs two atoms share, the more electron density sits between the nuclei, and the harder those nuclei get pulled toward each other.

Nitrogen gas, N2, is the textbook triple bond molecule. Each nitrogen atom brings 5 valence electrons, for a total of 10. If the two nitrogens share three pairs, 6 electrons, in a triple bond, that leaves 4 electrons, exactly enough for one lone pair on each nitrogen. Check each atom's octet: a nitrogen in the structure N triple bonded to N counts all six electrons of the triple bond, since it touches all three shared pairs, plus its own lone pair, for 6 plus 2 equals 8 electrons. Both atoms are satisfied, and all 10 valence electrons are accounted for.

Triple bonds are not limited to two identical atoms. Acetylene, C2H2, has the skeleton H-C triple bond C-H. Counting valence electrons: each carbon contributes 4 and each hydrogen contributes 1, for a total of 2 times 4 plus 2 times 1, or 10. Two C-H single bonds use 4 electrons, and the C-C triple bond uses the remaining 6. Each carbon counts 2 electrons from its C-H bond plus 6 from the triple bond, for a full octet of 8, with no lone pairs needed on either carbon. This is why acetylene is a straight, linear molecule around each carbon.

Triple bonds are shorter and considerably stronger than single or double bonds between the same two elements, and that strength has real consequences. The nitrogen-nitrogen triple bond in N2 is one of the strongest bonds known, which is exactly why atmospheric nitrogen is so chemically unreactive even though it makes up about 78 percent of the air. Breaking that bond to make nitrogen available for proteins and DNA requires either lightning, industrial catalysts under high pressure and temperature in the Haber-Bosch process, or specialized bacterial enzymes, all of which supply enough energy to pull the three shared pairs apart.

Three shared pairs is the practical maximum for the covalent bonds you will draw between typical nonmetal atoms in a simple Lewis structure. Carbon monoxide, CO, is another common example: with 10 valence electrons total, its most reasonable Lewis structure is a carbon triple bonded to oxygen, with one lone pair on each atom, similar in electron count to N2. As you will see in later sections on formal charge, checking whether a triple bond makes sense for a given molecule often requires more than just satisfying octets.
